delegated_acts.title: Technical Descriptions of Product Categories (Annex III and IV)
delegated_acts.covers: Technical descriptions of important (Class I/II) and critical product categories — determines which conformity assessment procedure applies

delegated_acts.title: Exclusion of Motor Vehicles from CRA Scope
delegated_acts.covers: Specifies that motor vehicles type-approved under UN R155/R156 are excluded from CRA where sectoral rules achieve equivalent cybersecurity level

delegated_acts.title: Conditions for Delaying Vulnerability Notification to CSIRTs
delegated_acts.covers: Circumstances under which manufacturer notification to CSIRT of actively exploited vulnerability may be delayed — security-sensitive disclosure

proportionality.description: CRA applies tiered obligations based on product risk classification (default, important Class I, important Class II, critical) and operator type (manufacturer, open-source steward, importer, distributor)

tiers.name: default
tiers.applies_to: All products with digital elements not listed in Annex III or IV
tiers.note: Essential cybersecurity requirements (Annex I) + self-assessment conformity (Module A, internal control). Majority of products fall here.

tiers.name: important_class_I
tiers.applies_to: Products in Annex III Class I (e.g., identity management, VPNs, network management, SIEM, boot managers, password managers, routers for industrial use)
tiers.note: Harmonised standard → self-assessment allowed. Otherwise third-party assessment (Module B+C or Module H) required. Art. 32(2)(a)/(b).

tiers.name: important_class_II
tiers.applies_to: Products in Annex III Class II (e.g., hypervisors, container runtimes, firewalls, tamper-resistant microprocessors, HSMs, smartcards, industrial IoT not covered by sectoral rules)
tiers.note: Mandatory third-party conformity assessment (Module B+C or Module H). No self-assessment shortcut.

tiers.name: critical
tiers.applies_to: Products in Annex IV (e.g., hardware devices with security boxes, smartcard readers, HSMs for qualified signatures, smart meter gateways)
tiers.note: Third-party assessment required. Commission may additionally require European cybersecurity certificate (EUCC) per Art. 8(1).

tiers.name: open_source_steward
tiers.applies_to: Legal persons systematically supporting FOSS development for commercial activities (Art. 3(14))
tiers.note: Reduced obligations: cybersecurity policy, vulnerability handling cooperation with CSIRTs, security attestation documentation. NOT subject to full manufacturer obligations.

tiers.name: sme_support
tiers.applies_to: Microenterprises, small and medium-sized enterprises, including start-ups
tiers.note: Commission and Member States must provide guidance and support. Conformity assessment bodies must consider proportionality of fees.

derogations.applies_to: Medical devices (MDR/IVDR), motor vehicles (2019/2144), aviation (2018/1139), marine equipment (2014/90/EU)
derogations.description: Products covered by these sectoral regulations are fully excluded from CRA scope

derogations.applies_to: Products covered by other Union rules achieving equivalent cybersecurity level
derogations.description: Commission may limit or exclude CRA application via delegated act where sectoral rules achieve same or higher protection

derogations.applies_to: Products with EU type-examination certificates issued before CRA application date
derogations.description: Transitional provision: existing certificates remain valid until expiry or 11 December 2029 at the latest

pitfalls.description: Support period is the EXPECTED product lifetime or 5 years from placing on market, WHICHEVER IS LONGER. Many assume a flat 5-year period. Art. 13(8) requires manufacturers to determine the expected product lifetime considering user expectations, product nature, and Union law. A router expected to be used for 10 years has a 10-year support period, not 5.

Actively exploited vulnerabilities must be reported to the designated CSIRT within 24 hours of awareness (early warning), then within 72 hours (vulnerability notification with initial assessment), then within 14 days (final report). This is separate from and in addition to NIS2 incident reporting. Many conflate the two timelines.

Annex I has TWO distinct parts: Part I covers product properties (security by design, default secure config, access control, data protection, availability, minimized attack surface), Part II covers manufacturer PROCESSES (vulnerability identification, documentation, SBOM, remediation without delay, testing). Compliance requires BOTH parts. Don't assess only product requirements.

SBOM must be generated but is NOT required to be made public. Art. 13(5) requires it to be included in technical documentation (Art. 31) and made available to market surveillance authorities on request. However, CSIRTs can request it under Art. 14(2)(c). Stating 'publish your SBOM' as a CRA requirement is wrong.

FOSS is only out of scope if provided outside 'commercial activity'. Recitals 18-20 clarify: charging for support/services, being provided by a commercial entity as part of its products, or accepting donations beyond hosting costs can bring FOSS into scope. The test is whether the software is 'intended for commercial activities' (Art. 3(14)), not whether money changes hands.

Important Class I products can self-assess if conformity is demonstrated using harmonised standards covering ALL essential requirements in Annex I. If harmonised standards only cover SOME requirements, third-party assessment is still needed for the uncovered parts. As of 2026, no harmonised standards have been published — meaning Class I currently requires third-party assessment in practice.

A 'substantial modification' (change affecting Annex I compliance or changing intended purpose) resets the conformity assessment obligation. Security patches and regular updates are NOT substantial modifications (Recital 42), but feature updates that alter the attack surface may be. This applies to the PERSON making the modification — an integrator who substantially modifies a component becomes the manufacturer for CRA purposes.

Art. 16 establishes a single reporting platform managed by ENISA for vulnerability and incident notifications. This is distinct from NIS2 reporting (national CSIRT) and GDPR breach notification (DPA). Manufacturers must report through this platform, not directly to national authorities. Platform operational by 11 September 2026.

cross_regulation.note: CRA and NIS2 have independent but related obligations. NIS2 covers operators; CRA covers product manufacturers. A company using a product may need NIS2 compliance while the product manufacturer needs CRA compliance. Vulnerability reporting timelines differ: CRA Art. 14 (24h/72h/14d) vs NIS2 Art. 23 (24h/72h/1 month). Both apply if the manufacturer is also a NIS2-essential entity.

AI systems classified as high-risk under AI Act that comply with CRA Annex I are deemed to meet AI Act Art. 15 cybersecurity requirements. CRA conformity assessment applies for the cybersecurity part, but AI Act conformity assessment still required for other AI-specific requirements.

EUCC certificates under Cybersecurity Act create presumption of conformity with CRA Annex I requirements. Critical products (Annex IV) may be required to hold EUCC certificates. Harmonised standards and EUCC are alternative conformity paths.

Revised Product Liability Directive covers damage caused by defective products including software. CRA conformity evidence is relevant to PLD defect assessment. Non-compliance with CRA essential requirements strengthens a PLD claim.

CRA Annex I Part I requires data protection by design (minimisation, encryption, access control). These overlap with GDPR Art. 25 (data protection by design) and Art. 32 (security of processing). CRA compliance contributes to but does not guarantee GDPR compliance.
RED delegated acts on cybersecurity (Art. 3(3)(d)(e)(f)) for radio equipment will be superseded by CRA requirements from the CRA application date. Transition period applies.

key_structures.title: Obligations of manufacturers — the core obligation article
key_structures.description: 19 paragraphs. Para 1-4: design and development against Annex I. Para 5: SBOM in technical documentation. Para 6: due diligence on components including FOSS. Para 7: coordinated vulnerability disclosure. Para 8: support period determination (expected lifetime or 5 years, whichever longer). Para 9-10: instructions for use and security information. Para 12: CE marking and EU declaration of conformity. Para 14: obligation to withdraw/recall non-compliant products. Para 15-16: cooperation with market surveillance authorities. Most compliance gaps are traceable to incomplete implementation of this article.

key_structures.title: Reporting obligations — three-stage notification
key_structures.description: Para 1: actively exploited vulnerability discovered. Para 2: three reports: (a) early warning within 24 hours, (b) vulnerability notification within 72 hours with initial assessment plus SBOM of affected components, (c) final report within 14 days. Para 3: incident reporting (separate from vulnerability). Para 4: possibility of delayed notification for security reasons. Para 8: CSIRT may request further information. Para 9: ENISA must forward to national CSIRTs and single points of contact.

key_structures.title: Conformity assessment procedures — risk-tiered
key_structures.description: Para 1: default products use internal control (Module A per Annex VII, Part I). Para 2: Important Class I use (a) harmonised standards + internal control OR (b) EU-type examination (Module B per Annex VII, Part II) + (c) compliance with type (Module C) OR (d) full QA (Module H per Annex VII, Part IV). Para 3: Important Class II and Critical always require (b)+(c) or (d). Para 4: prior existing certificates. Para 5: notified body involvement for Class I without full harmonised standard coverage.

key_structures.title: Obligations of open-source software stewards — the FOSS framework
key_structures.description: Para 1: cybersecurity policy for secure development. Para 2: cooperate with CSIRTs on vulnerability handling. Para 3: facilitate voluntary security attestation (Art. 25). Stewards are NOT manufacturers — they have reduced obligations. Key distinction from manufacturer obligations: no conformity assessment, no CE marking, no recall obligation.

key_recitals.clarifies: Scope of 'product with digital elements' — includes standalone software. Even software distributed without hardware is in scope if it has a direct or indirect data connection.

FOSS scope — software developed in the course of commercial activity IS in scope. 'Commercial activity' characterized by: charging for technical support, providing a paid software platform incorporating FOSS, monetizing personal data.

FOSS out-of-scope conditions — not-for-profit FOSS development, academic research, and pre-release contributions (bug fixes, feedback) to FOSS projects are NOT commercial activity even when contributed by commercial entities.

Annex I Part I essential requirements — security by design principle explained: protection against unauthorized access, confidentiality of stored/transmitted data, availability and resilience, minimized attack surface, impact limitation of incidents. These are outcome-based, not prescriptive.

Security updates are NOT substantial modifications — a regular security patch does not trigger a new conformity assessment. But an update that changes the intended purpose or affects Annex I compliance IS a substantial modification.

Vulnerability handling processes — Annex I Part II requires documented processes, not just ad-hoc responses. Must include: testing for vulnerabilities (including known ones), remediation without delay, public disclosure policies.

national_implementation.pattern: CRA is a regulation (directly applicable). Member States designate market surveillance authorities (Art. 52) and notifying authorities (Art. 36). Search Law MCPs for national implementing measures.

known_examples.note: BSI designated as market surveillance authority for CRA in Germany. Existing BSI cybersecurity certification infrastructure leveraged.

evidence_hint: Call get_evidence_requirements(regulation='CRA') for per-article audit artifacts. Key artifacts: SBOM (Art. 13(5)), Technical Documentation (Art. 31), EU Declaration of Conformity (Art. 28), Vulnerability Handling Process documentation (Art. 13(6), Annex I Part II), Support Period determination justification (Art. 13(8)), Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure policy (Art. 13(7)).

citation_format: Cite as: CRA Art. X(Y) for main regulation. For Annex references: CRA Annex N, Part X. For delegated/implementing acts: Commission Delegated/Implementing Regulation (EU) YYYY/NNNN, Art. X.
